hints: Look at the black bars in Fig. 2.1 from Na to Cl and note the direction of change, then think about what is added to the atom as proton number increases across the same period.
Think about whether electrons are added to a new shell across Period 3, and what this means for shielding compared with the change in protons.
walkthrough:
See the pattern in the black bars**
Picture yourself moving from Na on the left to Cl on the right. The black bars get shorter, so atoms get smaller. All these atoms have their outer electrons in the n = 3 shell, so you are not adding a new shell.

Count what changes in the nucleus**
Each step to the right adds one proton, so nuclear charge rises from +11 in Na to +17 in Cl. The inner shells stay the same (1s, 2s, 2p), so extra 3s and 3p electrons shield very poorly. Shielding stays approximately constant.

Link stronger pull to smaller size**
With more protons pulling on the same shell and almost no extra shielding, the effective attraction on the outer electrons increases. The electron shell is drawn closer to the nucleus, so atomic radius decreases.

Final answer: Atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl.
Nuclear charge increases across the period with similar shielding, so there is greater attraction of the outer electrons to the nucleus.

hints: Write the electron configurations of Al and P, then work out what each must do to achieve a stable octet, loss or gain of electrons.
Compare the number of occupied shells left after Al forms its ion with the number of shells still occupied after P forms its ion.
walkthrough:
Form the two ions in your head**
$\text{Al}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^1$. It loses its three outer electrons to leave the stable $2,8$ arrangement, giving $\text{Al}^{3+}$. $\text{P}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$. It gains three electrons to complete the octet, giving $2,8,8$ in $\text{P}^{3-}$.

See why losing shrinks and gaining swells**
When $\text{Al}$ loses the whole n = 3 shell, the ion has only two occupied shells, so the radius collapses to about 50 pm. When $\text{P}$ gains electrons, it keeps all three shells and extra electron repulsion expands the cloud, giving a radius over 200 pm.

Explain the jump in Fig. 2.1**
That is why the white bar drops very low for $\text{Al}$ and jumps very high for $\text{P}$. The large difference is not a gradual trend, it is a switch from a cation with n = 2 as the outer shell to an anion with n = 3 as the outer shell.

Final answer: $\text{Al}$ loses 3 electrons to form $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{P}$ gains 3 electrons to form $\text{P}^{3-}$.
$\text{Al}^{3+}$ has one fewer occupied shell than $\text{P}^{3-}$, so it is much smaller.

hints: For row A, use oxygen as -2 in each oxide formula to calculate the oxidation number of the Period 3 element, remembering $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ has two Na atoms and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ has four P atoms.
For row B, recall how basic oxides give high pH, amphoteric and insoluble oxides give no pH, and acidic non-metal oxides give low pH.
walkthrough:
Work out oxidation numbers quickly**
Take O as -2. In $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $2 \times \text{Na} + (-2) = 0$ so Na is +1. In MgO, Mg is +2. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is given as +3. In $\text{SiO}_2$, Si + $2(-2) = 0$ so Si is +4. In $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $4 \times \text{P} + 10(-2) = 0$ so P is +5. In $\text{SO}_3$, S is +6.

Link oxide type to pH**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is strongly basic and dissolves to give $\text{NaOH}$, pH about 13. MgO is sparingly soluble and weakly basic, pH about 9. $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ forms $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and $\text{SO}_3$ forms $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, both strongly acidic with pH 0 to 2. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ do not dissolve, so no pH is recorded.

Final answer: Row A (oxidation number): $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ +1, MgO +2, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ +3, $\text{SiO}_2$ +4, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ +5, $\text{SO}_3$ +6.
Row B (pH): $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ 12-14, MgO 8-10, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ -, $\text{SiO}_2$ -, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ 0-4, $\text{SO}_3$ 0-4.

hints: Think about what must happen before a pH value can be measured when an oxide is added to water.
walkthrough:
Why a dash means no solution**
A pH meter measures $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ in aqueous solution. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ has a strong ionic lattice with high lattice energy and $\text{SiO}_2$ has a giant covalent lattice, neither breaks up in water. With no dissolved ions and no reaction, there is simply no solution to test.
Final answer: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ are insoluble in water, so no solution forms.

hints: Treat $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ as a basic oxide that reacts with acid to make a salt plus water, then balance Na, Cl, H and O.
walkthrough:
Build a simple base plus acid equation**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ acts as a base. With $\text{HCl}$ it gives the salt $\text{NaCl}$ plus water. You need two $\text{HCl}$ to supply two $\text{Cl}$ for two $\text{Na}$ and two H for $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: $$\text{Na}_2\text{O} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Remember $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric so it reacts with a base, here $\text{NaOH}$, to give sodium aluminate $\text{NaAlO}_2$ plus water, then balance Al and Na.
walkthrough:
Use the amphoteric character**
$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ reacts with both acids and bases. With $\text{NaOH}$ it forms the aluminate ion $\text{AlO}_2^-$, seen as $\text{NaAlO}_2$, plus water. Balancing gives two $\text{Na}$ and two $\text{Al}$ on each side: $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAlO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Think about how cation size changes down Group 2 and how easily a smaller, more polarising cation distorts the nitrate ion on heating.
walkthrough:
Picture stability going down the group**
Going down from $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ to $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$, the cation gets larger and less polarising, so it distorts the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion less. More heat is needed to decompose the nitrate, so stability increases down the group.
Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2.

hints: Recall the general equation for Group 2 nitrate decomposition: nitrate gives oxide plus two gases, one brown and one that relights a glowing splint.
walkthrough:
Name the two gases**
All Group 2 nitrates decompose in the same way, for example: $$2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$ Besides the solid oxide, the products are nitrogen dioxide, $\text{NO}_2$, the brown gas, and oxygen, $\text{O}_2$.
